title: THE CHURCH THAT HAD SPIRITUAL GIFTS—AND A SEXUAL SCANDAL SO BAD EVEN PAUL WAS SHOCKED
paragraphs: THE CHURCH THAT HAD SPIRITUAL GIFTS—AND A SEXUAL SCANDAL SO BAD EVEN PAUL WAS SHOCKED

They had spiritual gifts. They knew Christian doctrine. They gathered in the name of Jesus. And inside their church was a sexual scandal so disturbing that Paul said even the surrounding pagan world would recoil from it. But perhaps the most frightening part of the story was not simply what one man was doing. It was what the church had learned to tolerate.
Imagine walking into the church at Corinth.
You might have been impressed.

People were spiritually gifted. There were powerful personalities, gifted speakers, manifestations of spiritual gifts, theological discussions, passionate gatherings, and believers who apparently considered themselves spiritually mature.
Paul himself acknowledged something extraordinary about them.
He told them they were “not lacking in any gift” while waiting for the revelation of Jesus Christ.
The Greek reads:
“ὥστε ὑμᾶς μὴ ὑστερεῖσθαι ἐν μηδενὶ χαρίσματι…”
Hōste hymas mē hystereisthai en mēdeni charismati…
The important word is χαρίσματι — charismati, from charisma: a gracious gift, a gift bestowed by grace.
Think about that.
This was not a spiritually empty congregation.
They had gifts.
And yet something horrifying was happening among them.
Something that should permanently destroy one of the most dangerous assumptions Christians can make:
That giftedness automatically proves godliness.
Because a person can be gifted and still need repentance.
A church can be charismatic and still be compromised.
People can speak beautifully about Jesus while secretly protecting what Jesus died to free them from.
You can know Scripture and still refuse to obey the Scripture you know.
You can raise your hands in worship while keeping part of your heart locked away from God.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not having no knowledge of God.
It is becoming so familiar with holy things that sin stops shocking you.
Then Paul receives the report.
And suddenly the tone changes.
“Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία…”
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you…”
Then Paul makes the accusation even more disturbing:
“…καὶ τοιαύτη πορνεία ἥτις οὐδὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν…”
…kai toiautē porneia hētis oude en tois ethnesin…
Sexual immorality of such a kind that it was not even among the Gentiles.
Then comes the sentence that must have fallen across the Corinthian gathering like a stone:
“…ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.”
A man had his father’s wife.
Notice the precision.
Paul says “his father’s wife.” The text does not tell us enough to identify her as the man’s biological mother, so we should not make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
But we do not need exaggeration.
What Paul actually says is already devastating.
There was open sexual immorality inside the congregation so scandalous that Paul compared it unfavorably with the surrounding pagan world.
And somehow…
the church had learned to live with it.
That is where this story stops being merely about ancient Corinth.
Because maybe you have never committed Corinth’s particular sin.
But perhaps you recognize Corinth’s greater temptation.
The ability to become comfortable around what God calls us to confront.
We rename things.
We soften things.
We manage appearances.
We protect reputations.
We tell ourselves, “God understands.”
We confuse grace with permission.
We confuse compassion with silence.
We confuse spiritual gifts with spiritual maturity.
And gradually something happens inside us.
What once convicted us becomes familiar.
What once made us tremble becomes manageable.
What once drove us to repentance becomes something we explain away.
That is how compromise grows.
Usually not with someone waking up one morning and deciding to abandon Christ.
It happens quietly.
One compromise.
Then another.
One hidden message.
One private browser window.
One relationship nobody knows about.
One financial lie.
One secret addiction.
One resentment we keep feeding.
One flirtation we insist is innocent.
One habit we promise God we will stop “soon.”
One apology we refuse to make.
One confession we keep postponing.
And eventually we learn how to worship while hiding.
That may be one of the most terrifying sentences in this entire article:
You can learn how to worship while hiding.
You can sing with tears in your eyes while protecting the very thing causing those tears.
You can post Bible verses while your private life is collapsing.
You can encourage everyone else while secretly wondering whether God still wants anything to do with you.
You can become so skilled at looking spiritually alive that nobody notices you are bleeding internally.
But Jesus notices.
And His response is not indifference.
It is love too holy to leave you there.
Paul tells the Corinthians something they desperately needed to hear:
“And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?”
That word changes everything.
Paul does not tell them to turn the scandal into entertainment.
He does not tell them to gossip.
He does not tell them to enjoy watching another believer fall.
He tells them to mourn.
Biblical confrontation should have tears in its eyes.
The church is not supposed to celebrate somebody’s destruction.
We are supposed to grieve sin because sin destroys people Christ came to save.
There is an enormous difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation says, “Look how disgusting you are.”
Conviction says, “Look where this road is taking you. Come home.”
Condemnation pushes the sinner toward despair.
Godly discipline aims toward repentance.
And that is why Paul’s instructions in 1 Corinthians 5 are severe.
He commands the church to remove the unrepentant offender from their fellowship.
To modern ears, that may sound cruel.
But Paul reveals something crucial about the purpose:
“…so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.”
Saved.
Do not miss that word.
Even in severe discipline, redemption remains on the horizon.
The objective is not humiliation for humiliation’s sake.
Not revenge.
Not religious superiority.
Not, “We are holy and you are filthy.”
The goal is that a sinner wakes up.
That deception breaks.
That repentance comes.
That a wandering person finally realizes how far from home he has traveled.
Because biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing what was necessary because sin matters eternally.
The cross proves both things at once.
Our sin is worse than we wanted to admit.
God's mercy is greater than we dared to imagine.
Look at Jesus.
The nails do not tell you sin is insignificant.
The nails tell you sin is deadly.
But the Savior hanging from those nails tells you sinners are loved beyond comprehension.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious cosmetics.
Death…
and resurrection.
Repentance…
and forgiveness.
Guilt exposed…
and guilt carried by Another.
This is why the Gospel refuses two equally destructive lies.
The first says:
“My sin is not that serious.”
The second says:
“My sin is too serious for Jesus.”
Both are lies.
Corinth destroys the first.
Calvary destroys the second.
And perhaps that is why somebody reading this right now feels uncomfortable.
Because this stopped being an article about Corinth several paragraphs ago.
Now there is something between you and God.
Something came to mind.
A name.
A conversation.
A habit.
A room.
A relationship.
A website.
A resentment.
A compromise.
A secret.
Something you desperately hoped this article would not touch.
You do not need to tell the internet every detail.
But you do need to stop lying to God.
He already knows.
And strangely enough, that is not the worst news you could receive tonight.
It may be the best.
Because the Jesus who knows everything about you is still calling you.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up sufficiently and perhaps Christ will receive you.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and those who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive forgiveness and new life.
Paul eventually reminds these same Corinthians of what grace had already done among them.
After listing patterns of sin that do not characterize those who inherit the kingdom of God, he says something breathtaking:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
There is an entire Gospel hidden inside that word.
You were.
But Jesus intervened.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
That means the church is not a museum displaying people who never became dirty.
It is a community of people whose only hope is that Jesus washes sinners.
There were people sitting in Corinth whose histories would have embarrassed them.
Sexual histories.
Idolatrous histories.
Greedy histories.
Drunken histories.
Exploitative histories.
Broken histories.
And Paul did not say:
“And such are you forever.”
He said:
“And such were some of you.”
That is what Jesus does.
He takes identity statements written by sin and turns them into past tense.
You were enslaved.
You were lost.
You were condemned.
You were living for yourself.
You were hiding.
You were running.
Then grace found you.
This does not mean believers become instantly flawless.
Sanctification is real, often painful, lifelong transformation.
But grace means your sin no longer gets the final authority to tell you who you are.
Jesus does.
And maybe that is what you desperately needed tonight.
Not permission to continue.
Not another excuse.
Not somebody telling you that rebellion does not matter.
You needed someone to love you enough to say:
Come out of hiding.
There is mercy here.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Bring it into the light.
Seek wise pastoral help and accountability where needed.

If another person has been harmed, do not use “grace” to escape responsibility. Repentance does not manipulate victims into silence, and church reputation must never become more important than protecting people who have been abused or exploited. Where crimes have occurred, spiritual language must never be used as a substitute for appropriate reporting to civil authorities.
Truth matters.
Justice matters.
Holiness matters.
And grace matters.
Because Jesus is not merely interested in making scandals disappear.
He wants people transformed.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe the people commenting “Amen” beneath your Christian posts would never imagine what you battle when the screen goes dark.
But secrecy cannot heal you.
Jesus can.
And there is something incredibly beautiful about the Gospel:
Jesus already knows the worst chapter.
And He still invites sinners to repent and come to Him.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples abandoned Him.
Paul once persecuted His people.
The Corinthian church became synonymous with dysfunction.
Yet none of those failures became greater than the grace of Christ.
This is not permission to sin.
It is permission to stop hiding.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need sophisticated theology.
Maybe it sounds more like:
“Jesus… I’m tired.”
“I have been pretending.”
“I keep returning to this.”
“I don't know how to stop.”
“I am ashamed.”
“I need You.”
“Forgive me.”
“Change me.”
That prayer, when it rises from genuine repentance and faith, is not beneath the attention of Christ.
He came for sinners.
The church at Corinth teaches us that spiritual activity can coexist with horrifying immaturity.
But the Gospel teaches us something greater:
Jesus does not merely expose what is broken.
He redeems people who surrender it to Him.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create spectators.
Not to manufacture religious outrage.
Not to collect Christians who simply agree with Christian content.
We want people opening Scripture again.
Praying again.
Repenting again.
Following Jesus when nobody is watching.
Helping exhausted believers return to truth.
Helping wounded believers remember grace.
Helping lukewarm Christians wake up.
Helping seekers discover that Christianity is not ultimately about religious performance but about Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
You do not have to publish the details.
Those three words are enough.
No more hiding.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need proof that Christians struggle, repent, fall, get back up, seek help, and discover that God's mercy has not disappeared.
Then do something else.
Not because an algorithm deserves it.
Because somebody you know may be hiding.
Someone may be one night away from giving up on church.
Someone may think their sexual past has permanently disqualified them from Jesus.
Someone may be confusing grace with permission.
Someone may desperately need both warning and hope.
If this truth glorifies God, help carry it beyond this page.
And yes, if you have an unbelieving friend who believes Christianity is only a collection of hypocrites pretending to be perfect, perhaps send this to them too.
Tell them:
We are not claiming Christians have never been broken.
We are claiming Jesus saves broken people.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction felt like yesterday.
Come back when compromise starts sounding reasonable.
Come back when shame tells you to hide.
Come back when you begin confusing spiritual gifts with spiritual maturity.
Come back and remember Corinth.
Then remember Calvary.
God's grace cannot be purchased, and no financial contribution earns spiritual merit.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can help this work continue reaching people with Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement, and the message of Jesus Christ.
Jesus is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Not a platform.
Jesus Christ.

If supporting this ministry helps us place His truth before one more wounded believer, one more wandering son, one more ashamed daughter, one more exhausted Christian, or one more person who has never understood the Gospel, then your support becomes part of helping carry that message farther.
But Christ receives the glory.
Always.
Corinth had gifts.
Corinth had knowledge.
Corinth had eloquence.
Corinth had spiritual experiences.
And Corinth still desperately needed repentance.
So do we.
The question is not whether you can point toward somebody else's scandal.
The question is what Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Because someday there will be no curated profile.
No reputation to protect.
No religious vocabulary to hide behind.
No audience to impress.
Just you…
and the Christ who already knows everything.
And if that frightens you, remember who that Christ is.
The One who was crucified for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who receives the repentant.
The One who washes.
The One who sanctifies.
The One who justifies.
The One who still transforms people everyone else has written off.
So bring Him the chapter you wish had never been written.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the wreckage.
Bring Him the person behind the Christian appearance.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after this screen goes dark:
The scandal may explain how you fell—but the scars in His hands tell you Who can still rewrite what comes next.
